name: Meradimate
lead: Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is an ester of anthranilic acid and menthol that acts as a UVA filter in sunscreens [1]. It is one of the 17 ingredients the US FDA lists for over-the-counter sunscreen products [1]. It should not be confused with methyl anthranilate [1].
Published research on it is mostly photophysical. A US label for a sports sunscreen lists it with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone [2].

For appearance, a UVA filter matters because UVA penetrates deeper than UVB and contributes to photoaging, so broad-spectrum sunscreen ingredients are part of how people protect their skin from sun-related lines, spots and tone changes; the sunscreen label listing meradimate states that, used with other sun protection, the product decreases the risk of early skin aging.[2]

paras: Studies report that menthyl anthranilate is strongly fluorescent in ethanol and characterise its excited states [3][4]. Work on the related methyl anthranilate examined its photoprotection mechanism [5], and another study found antioxidants suppressed singlet-oxygen generation sensitised by menthyl anthranilate [6].

In cell studies chemical filters showed contradictory effects in UV/ROS-stressed keratinocytes and fibroblasts [7]. A study of UV filters and human sperm found several filters mimicked progesterone-like calcium signalling through CatSper channels [8]. These are laboratory findings, not clinical outcomes.

A DailyMed sunscreen label listing meradimate states that it helps prevent sunburn and, with other sun protection measures, decreases the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging; it warns users to stop use and ask a doctor if rash occurs [2].

Menthyl anthranilate has the formula C17H25NO2 and a molar mass of about 275.4 g/mol, and is known by names including meradimate, menthyl-o-aminobenzoate and anthranilic acid menthyl ester.[1] Wikipedia lists it among UVA filters, using a UVA range of 315 to 400 nm, and says the US FDA recognises it as one of 17 over-the-counter sunscreen ingredients; it also appears in lists of sunscreening agents approved by one or more agencies such as the FDA, the EU's SCCS and Australia's TGA.[1]

It is typically one of several actives in a US sunscreen. The label for a sports sunscreen lists it together with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone, with the usual directions for external use and warnings to stop use if a rash occurs.[2] An analytical method paper describes screening cosmetics for 16 UV filters by liquid chromatography, a reminder that filters are routinely monitored in finished products.[9]

sections.h: Photophysics and function as a filter
paras: Photophysical studies explain why an anthranilate can work as a filter: after absorbing UVA it releases the energy through fluorescence and other relaxation pathways rather than staying in a reactive state. A 2000 study measured a fluorescence quantum yield of about 0.64 in ethanol with emission in the 390 to 405 nm range, and detected phosphorescence in frozen solvent glasses; a 2013 study determined the lowest excited singlet and triplet state energies.[3][4]

Work on the related methyl anthranilate used wavepacket methods to examine its photoprotection mechanism,[5] and another study found that the antioxidants Trolox and alpha-tocopherol suppressed singlet oxygen sensitised by menthyl anthranilate.[6]

A 2023 report in Dermatitis described photoallergic contact dermatitis to menthyl anthranilate (meradimate), a skin reaction in which sun exposure triggers an immune response to the ingredient.[10] The sunscreen label advises stopping use and asking a doctor if a rash occurs.[2]

sections.h: How it helps skin look better
paras: Meradimate is a UVA filter, one ingredient in a sunscreen that blocks part of the ultraviolet spectrum. The appearance payoff comes from what UV exposure does over time: UVA reaches deep into the skin and, unlike UVB, produces little reddening while contributing to long-term damage, which is why dermatology references describe broad-spectrum protection as protection against both wavelength bands.[11] In a 2013 Australian trial of about 900 people, those who applied broad-spectrum sunscreen daily for four and a half years had smoother, more resilient skin than controls, and a small study of 32 subjects found improvement in photoaging signs with daily SPF 30 use over 12 weeks, according to the reference summary.[11] Those studies tested whole sunscreen products, not meradimate alone.

Meradimate itself absorbs in the shorter UVA range, so formulators typically combine it with other filters to cover the spectrum; the sunscreen label in the references lists it with octinoxate, octisalate and oxybenzone.[2][1]

In the United States sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs rather than cosmetics, which makes approval of new filters slow; the European Union treats them as cosmetics and lists more permitted filters, about 29 compared with about 17 in the US as of 2023 according to the summary.[11] Since 2019 the US Food and Drug Administration has been sorting the older filters into categories reflecting whether they are generally recognised as safe and effective, and in the summary's account only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide had been placed in the fully recognised category by 2021.[11] FDA absorption studies found that several organic filters pass into the bloodstream, which led the agency to request further safety data; the agency has not concluded that these ingredients are unsafe.[11]
Meradimate appears in the US monograph list of permitted UVA filters, as noted in encyclopedia entries on the compound.[1]

Meradimate is typically one ingredient among several filters rather than a headline active. Its label wording is standardised: products state that, used with other sun-protection measures, sunscreen decreases the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging, and they advise stopping use and consulting a doctor if a rash develops.[2]

card.summary: Older US-listed anthranilate UVA sunscreen filter, studied mostly for its photophysics.
card.note: Lab findings only; no dedicated clinical trials found.

quick.overview:
Meradimate (menthyl anthranilate) is a UVA filter listed among the FDA's OTC sunscreen ingredients and used in some products alongside other filters.

Research on it is mainly photophysical and in vitro.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVA light and has been characterised as fluorescent, with studies mapping its excited-state behaviour.
quick.risks: Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs. Lab studies have examined cell effects and sperm-signalling interactions of UV filters; no clinical outcome data were found.
